name: Small Universes
description: A Friedmann universe whose space is a torus or another quotient of flat or hyperbolic space, made by declaring points a fixed step apart to be one point. At each point its geometry is Friedmann's, its volume can be finite with no curvature to close it, and an observer sees each galaxy many times over, at a different age each time. George Ellis reviewed such universes in 1971, and with G. Schreiber named them small universes in 1986.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the drawings of the torus take its three periods equal to one length $L$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The ship in an old video game flies off the right edge of the screen and comes back in on the left, and the screen is flat the whole way across [levin2002]. A cube whose opposite faces are joined in the same way is a 3-torus, a space of finite volume with no wall anywhere, and whoever lives in it "has the illusion of seeing an infinite 3-dimensional lattice of images of himself" [levin2002]. The picture is Karl Schwarzschild's, from a lecture to the Astronomische Gesellschaft in Heidelberg on 9 August 1900 about how much curvature the astronomy of his day allowed space [kragh2012, schwarzschild1900]. He supposed that astronomers had found "countless identical copies of our Milky Way", one in each cube of a lattice that fills space [schwarzschild1998, luminet1999]. "We would be much happier with the view that these repetitions are illusory, that in reality space has peculiar connection properties so that if we leave any one cube through a side, then we immediately reenter it through the opposite side" [schwarzschild1998, luminet1999].¶Does general relativity mind? Einstein's equations are differential equations, and so "they describe only local properties of spacetime" [lachiezerey1995]. One metric that solves them "may correspond to different models of the Universe with different spatial topologies" [lachiezerey1995]. When Alexander Friedmann found the universe of negative curvature in 1924 he said as much: "To definitely decide about its finiteness one needs additional conditions" [friedmann1924, luminet2007]. He named what an astronomer in a glued universe would meet: "ghosts", which are "objects and their own images" [friedmann1924, luminet2007].¶The question came back on 18 May 1970, at a seminar in Gwatt on the bearings of topology upon general relativity, where George Ellis read a review of topology and cosmology [ellis1971]. "The essence of the study of cosmology", he said, "is trying to determine not merely possible space-time structures, but ones that probably exist in the universe" [ellis1971]. He set out which spaces of three dimensions a cosmologist can use and began to work out what an observer in a toroidal universe would see [luminet1999]. Flat space comes in 18 forms, ten of them closed and six of those orientable, and the simplest closed one is the 3-torus, with $x$, $y$, and $z$ each periodic [lachiezerey1995, zeldovich1984]. Each carries Friedmann's metric at every point, and the gluing takes away symmetry: the torus is "globally anisotropic even though the geometry of the metric is still locally isotropic" [levin2002]. It picks out a state of rest as well, so that twins who part and meet again with neither turning round agree on who is older, by "a preferred frame singled out by the topology of the space" [barrow2001].¶How would anyone know? In a universe smaller than the distance light has travelled since the big bang, the light of one galaxy reaches us along many routes, each wound a different number of times round, so the galaxy stands at many places on the sky and at a different age in each [lachiezerey1995]. To D. D. Sokolov and V. F. Shvartsman the copies were ghosts, and in 1974 they set lower limits on the size of the universe: its largest and smallest "gluing parameters" are no smaller than 400 and 10 megaparsecs [sokolov1974]. J. Richard Gott III found no cluster of galaxies twice in the counts of Shane and Wirtanen, and in 1980 put the radius of the cell above 400 megaparsecs for a Hubble constant of 50 km/s per megaparsec [gott1980]. The name came in 1986 from Ellis and G. Schreiber: "It is possible that we live in a 'small universe', that is, we might have seen round the universe many times since decoupling so that there are many images of each galaxy" [ellis1986, lachiezerey1995].¶A flat torus "can be made infinitesimally small", and negatively curved space allows no such freedom [levin2002]. A closed hyperbolic space of a given shape comes in one size: by G. D. Mostow's rigidity theorem its volume and the lengths of its closed geodesics "are topological invariants", fixed in units of the radius of curvature $a$ [mostow1968, lachiezerey1995]. The smallest is the Weeks manifold, of volume $0.9427\,a^3$, which David Gabai, Robert Meyerhoff, and Peter Milley proved in 2009 to be "the unique smallest volume closed orientable hyperbolic 3-manifold" [luminet1999, gabai2009]. Sokolov returned to the hyperbolic case with A. A. Starobinskii in 1975: "every spliced hyperbolic universe is globally inhomogeneous", its circuits shorter at some places than at others [sokolov1975]. Their example is a horn, hyperbolic space with two of its directions rolled up, where the circuits shrink without limit toward one end [sokolov1975].¶From the anisotropy of the microwave background, Daniel Stevens, Douglas Scott, and Joseph Silk found in 1993 that a cubic torus is at least $2400\,h^{-1}$ megaparsecs across, "80% of the horizon scale, implying that a topologically 'small' universe is no longer an interesting cosmological model" [stevens1993]. Neil J. Cornish, David N. Spergel, and Glenn D. Starkman worked out in 1998 what to look for: the microwave background comes to us from a sphere, a small universe makes that sphere cross its own copies, and "these intersections will be circles, regardless of the background geometry or topology" [cornish1998]. A small space of positive curvature, built on a dodecahedron, was the proposal of Jean-Pierre Luminet, Jeffrey R. Weeks, Alain Riazuelo, Roland Lehoucq, and Jean-Philippe Uzan in 2003 for the weak correlations of the microwave sky at wide angles [luminet2003]. Cornish, Spergel, and Starkman, with Eiichiro Komatsu, looked for pairs of matching circles in the first year of data from the WMAP satellite, found none wider than 25°, and for a wide class of models ruled out "a universe with topology scale smaller than 24 Gpc" [cornish2004]. The Planck maps of 2015 put the radius of the largest sphere that fits inside a cubic torus above 0.97 of the distance to the surface the radiation left [planck2016topology]. The circles test only the shortest loop through our own position, and in 2023 Pip Petersen and the COMPACT collaboration concluded that "a broader range of manifolds is observationally allowed than widely appreciated" [petersen2023].

related.text: The same universe before any points are identified. Every local measurement agrees with Friedmann's, and the two differ in topology alone [lachiezerey1995].
The hyperbolic small universe with nothing in it, $a = ct$. At each point it is Milne's universe, a piece of flat spacetime.

Universes on the same 3-torus, filled with gravitational waves in place of matter. With matter added, the Gowdy universes that are the same at every point include the flat Friedmann universe on a torus [martinbenito2011].

Homogeneous universes that expand at different rates in different directions. A torus has no isotropy to lose, and Ya. B. Zel'dovich and A. A. Starobinskii put such a universe on one in 1984 [zeldovich1984].

De Sitter space folded onto itself by its antipodal map, as flat space is folded here by translations. Willem de Sitter proposed the folded sphere for the space of the universe in 1917 [desitter1917, lachiezerey1995].
A universe that is finite because its space curves round into a sphere. A small universe is finite by the way its space is connected, with no curvature needed to close it [lachiezerey1995].
Flat spacetime with events identified under a boost, as space is identified here under translations. Misner's identification makes closed timelike curves, and the torus makes none [misner1967].
The horn's coordinates with $y$ and $z$ left open and the matter drifting along $x$. Farnsworth's dust is the open universe of dust given such a tilt [anton2023].

coordinates.name: Comoving Torus

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), dimensionless; the volume of space is $a^3L_1L_2L_3$
Period of $x$, a comoving length: the events $(t, x, y, z)$ and $(t, x + L_1, y, z)$ are one event, and the circle of $x$ has the length $aL_1$
Period of $y$, a comoving length; the circle of $y$ has the length $aL_2$
Period of $z$, a comoving length; the circle of $z$ has the length $aL_3$

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and comoving Cartesian coordinates $(x, y, z)$, each a length and periodic, with periods $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_3$. The scale factor $a(t) > 0$ is dimensionless. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Conformal Time on the Torus

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), dimensionless; the volume of space is $a^3L_1L_2L_3$
Period of $x$, a comoving length: the events $(t, x, y, z)$ and $(t, x + L_1, y, z)$ are one event, and the circle of $x$ has the length $aL_1$
Period of $y$, a comoving length; the circle of $y$ has the length $aL_2$
Period of $z$, a comoving length; the circle of $z$ has the length $aL_3$

coordinates.convention: We use the conformal time $\eta$, a length with $a\,d\eta = c\,dt$, and the comoving Cartesian coordinates $(x, y, z)$ of the torus, periodic with periods $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_3$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Comoving Hyperbolic
domains: (t, p) \sim (t, \gamma p) \;\text{(every } \gamma \text{ of a discrete group of isometries of hyperbolic space that moves every point } p\text{)}

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the time $t$; the volume of space is $a^3$ times a number its topology fixes

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and polar coordinates $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ about one observer, with $a\chi$ the distance from that observer. Two points $p$ and $\gamma p$ of hyperbolic space are one point of the universe for every $\gamma$ of a discrete group of its isometries that moves every point. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Horn

parameters.description: Scale factor ($a > 0$), a length, the radius of curvature of space at the time $t$
Period of $y$, a number: the events $(t, x, y, z)$ and $(t, x, y + b_2, z)$ are one event, and the circle of $y$ at $x$ has the length $ab_2e^{-x}$
Period of $z$, a number; the circle of $z$ at $x$ has the length $ab_3e^{-x}$

coordinates.convention: We use cosmic time $t$ and the coordinates $(x, y, z)$ of Sokolov and Starobinsky, each a number: $ax$ is the distance along the horn, and $y$ and $z$ are flat coordinates on the surfaces of constant $x$, periodic with periods $b_2$ and $b_3$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, a prime is the derivative along that chart time, $a' = da/d(ct)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
